LIME

An explanation model

  • •Goal: explain the output of any machine learning model by attributing         feature’s contribution to a prediction. 

    • •For a simple model : the model itself; it perfectly represents itself and is easy to understand.  

    • •For complex models (as ensemble methods, deep networks): we cannot use the original model as its own best explanation because it is not easy to understand. 

  • •A simpler explanation model (g), which we define as any interpretable approximation of the original model (f). 

Additive feature attribution methods

  • •  

How would a given example score differently if it had different attributes?

  Local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) for explaining model predictions

iris example

  • •A dataset of petal (花瓣) and sepal (萼片) measurements for three varieties of iris. 

  • •The object is to predict whether a given iris is a setosa based on its petal and sepal dimensions. 

    • •4 measurements 

      • •sepal length 

      • •sepal width 

      • •petal length 

      • •petal width 

    • •3 different species  

      • •setosa 

      • •versicolor  

      • •virginica  

Loading the iris dataset : LIME.R

iris <- iris

iris$class <- as.numeric(iris$Species == "setosa")

set.seed(2345)

intrain <- runif(nrow(iris)) < 0.75

train <- iris[intrain,]

test <- iris[!intrain,]

Fitting a XGBOOST model to the iris training data

source("lime_iris_example.R")

input <- as.matrix(train[, 1:4])

model <- fit_iris_example(input, train$class)

Building a LIME explainer from the model and training data

library(lime)

explainer <- lime(train[,1:4],

                      model = model,

                      bin_continuous = TRUE,

                      n_bins = 10)

Use 10 bins, Bins the continuous variables when making explanations

How does LIME work?

Toy example to present intuition for LIME

  • •The black-box model’s complex decision function f (unknown to LIME) is represented by the blue/pink background, which cannot be approximated well by a linear model.  

  • •The bold red cross is the instance being explained.  

  • •LIME samples instances, gets predictions using f, and weighs them by the proximity to the instance being explained (represented here by size). => The dashed line is the learned explanation that is locally (but not globally) faithful. 

Notional sketch of how LIME works

Synthetic data points

  • •original data point  

Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width

Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width

The model’s decision surface

  • •LIME’s estimate of the decision surface near the example we are trying to explain. 

  • •Fit an m-dimensional linear model for {yi} as a function of {si}. The linear model is LIME’s estimate of the original model’s decision surface near example (a dashed line).  

LIME

  • •interprets individual model predictions based on locally approximating the model around a given prediction 

  • •A mapping function x = hx(x′) converts a binary vector of interpretable inputs into the original input space. 

    • •For bag of words text features: a vector of 1’s or 0’s (present or not) => the original word count if the simplified input is one, or zero if the simplified input is zero.  

    • •For images: image as a set of super pixels 

      • •Map 1 to leaving the super pixel as its original value 

      • •Map 0 to replacing the super pixel with an average of neighboring pixels (this is meant to represent being missing).

SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)

Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S. I. (2017). A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NeurIPS 2017), 4765-4774.

Shapley values

  • •The Shapley value comes from cooperative game theory and represents a fair way to distribute the gain (or payout) among the features (players) based on their contribution to the outcome.  

  • •In machine learning, it quantifies each feature’s contribution to a model’s prediction. 

    • •assign credit to each feature by averaging over all possible feature coalitions. 

SHapley Additive exPlanations(SHAP)

  • •SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. 

  • •Shapley regression values 

Kernel SHAP

  • •This algorithm estimates SHAP values by treating the model as a black box and using weighted linear regression over perturbed samples.  

  • •Understand the algorithm base on the code (Python) 

    • •Find a script for Kernel SHAP @ https://github.com/shap/shap? 

shap/explainers/_kernel.py

<number>

Pseudocode

  1. 1..For each instance to explain: def explain(self, incoming_instance, **kwargs) 

    • •Identify which features differ from background. 

    • •For all (or sampled) subsets of these features: 

      • •Construct synthetic samples by combining instance and background values. 

      • •Evaluate the model on these samples. self.run() 

    • •Use weighted linear regression to attribute the output difference to each feature (the SHAP value). self.solve(self.nsamples / self.max_samples, d) 

  1. 1..Return a vector of SHAP values per feature, summing to the prediction minus the expected value. 

explain(self, incoming_instance, **kwargs)

  • •Find Varying Features 

    • •The method identifies which features in the instance differ from the background data (self.varying_groups). Only those need to be explained. 

  • •Cases 

    • •If no features vary: All SHAP values are zero. 

    • •If only one feature varies: All the difference is assigned to that feature. 

    • •If multiple features vary:  

      • •The algorithm enumerates or samples subsets of features (called "coalitions” of included/masked features). 

        • •Each sample : a binary vector z∈{0,1}M 

          • •zj=1: feature j is present 

          • •0: replaced with background. 

      • •For each subset, it creates a synthetic sample by combining the instance’s values for the included features and background data for the others. self.addsample() 

run(self)

  • •The model is evaluated on each synthetic sample to see how the presence/absence of feature groups changes the output. 

solve(self, fraction_evaluated, dim)
